outcome_detail: Federal jury verdict of $1 million against the City of New Orleans on August 21, 2024, after a three-day trial in the Eastern District of Louisiana; the jury found the city's hiring and inadequate supervision of the officer showed deliberate indifference to the plaintiff's civil rights. Plaintiff's attorneys had asked for $8 million. Some syndicated coverage reported a total award of $1.6 million. No appeal outcome found.
criminal_detail: Rodney Vicknair was federally charged in September 2022 with a civil rights violation (18 U.S.C. 242) for the sexual assault; he pleaded guilty and was sentenced on March 14, 2023 to 14 years in federal prison after the judge rejected a seven-year plea recommendation as unjustifiably lenient. NOPD had fired him in 2021. Vicknair died in federal custody on New Year's Day 2024, at age 57.
description: In May 2020, NOPD officer Rodney Vicknair was assigned to escort a 14-year-old girl to a hospital for a forensic exam after she was sexually assaulted by another man. Vicknair gave the girl his phone number, offered to be her friend and mentor, and groomed her over the following months, frequently appearing at her home; on September 23, 2020, when she was 15, he sexually assaulted her — conduct he later admitted in a federal guilty plea. In February 2021, the girl's family sued Vicknair, the City of New Orleans and others in federal court, alleging civil rights violations, assault and battery, and emotional distress, and asserting the city let him respond to a child sexual assault survivor despite prior complaints including predatory behavior toward women. In August 2024, a federal jury ordered the city to pay $1 million, finding its vetting and supervision of Vicknair deliberately indifferent. Vicknair was sentenced to 14 years in prison in March 2023 and died in custody in January 2024.

confidence_notes: Seed year hint was 2022, but reporting indicates the civil suit was filed in February 2021 (one outlet described it as 'the 2021 lawsuit'); year_filed set to 2021 accordingly. An NZ Herald syndication of the Washington Post story headlined the award as $1.6 million, versus $1 million in AP/WaPo/WWL headlines — the discrepancy (possibly an additional judgment against Vicknair or his estate) could not be confirmed, so the verdict amount is recorded per the dominant $1 million reporting. The Washington Post source article is paywalled; details were corroborated via AP and local coverage. Appeal status after the August 2024 verdict could not be confirmed.
